title: Double Integral
body:
$$
\iint_{R}f(x,y)dA
$$

---

Integrate over a **region of the plane** rather than an interval on a line. A single
[[Integral]] adds up $f(x)\,dx$, a strip of height $f$ and width $dx$; a double integral adds up
$f(x,y)\,dA$, a column of height $f$ standing on a patch of area $dA$. So
$\iint_R f\,dA$ is the **volume** under the surface $z = f(x,y)$ over $R$, and
$\iint_R 1\,dA$ is just the area of $R$.

MRU splits the multiple-integration material across two courses: **double integrals are taught
here in [[CALCULUS 2]], triple integrals in [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]]**. See
[[Multiple Integration]] for the general case. That is an unusual split and worth knowing, since
the obvious guess is that both live with the vector calculus.

## Iterated integrals

You never evaluate a double integral directly. **Fubini's theorem** says it equals an iterated
integral: integrate in one variable while treating the other as a constant, then integrate the
result. That inner step is a [[Partial Derivative|partial]] operation run backwards.

$$
\iint_R f(x,y)\,dA = \int_a^b\!\!\int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)} f(x,y)\,dy\,dx
$$

**Read the limits from the inside out.** The inner limits may depend on the outer variable; the
outer limits must be constants. If your outer limits still contain a variable, the setup is wrong.

Over a rectangle the limits are all constants and the order does not matter at all. Over a general
region it matters a great deal in practice, because one order may need the region split into two
pieces while the other does not, and one order may be elementary while the other is not.

**Changing the order of integration** is therefore a real technique rather than a curiosity:
redraw the region, re-read the limits in the other direction, and rewrite. The classic case is
$\int_0^1\!\!\int_y^1 e^{x^2}dx\,dy$, which is impossible as written because $e^{x^2}$ has no
elementary antiderivative, and becomes routine once the order is swapped.

## Polar coordinates

When the region is a disk, an annulus, or a sector, switch to [[Polar Coordinates]]. The area
element is **not** $dr\,d\theta$:

$$
dA = r\,dr\,d\theta
$$

The extra $r$ is there because a polar patch is a circular wedge whose width grows with the
distance from the origin, the same $\frac12 r^2$ reasoning as polar area. Forgetting it is the
standard error, and it is what a Jacobian accounts for in general (that machinery belongs to
[[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]]).

This is how the Gaussian integral $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}dx = \sqrt{\pi}$ is finally
evaluated: square it into a double integral over the plane, convert to polar, and the stray $r$
supplies exactly the factor that makes the [[Improper Integral]] solvable. The result underwrites
the [[Normal Distribution]] in [[STATISTICS]].
